1. Change **Name**, **Email**, **Role** or **Active**. Change **Role** to promote a member to admin or demote an admin to member.
1. Select **Save changes**.

DAIV keeps at least one active admin. You cannot deactivate your own account, and you cannot demote or delete the last active admin: promote another user first.

### Deactivate a user

Deactivate a user when you may want to restore their access later.

1. Under **Admin** → **Users**, select the user.
1. Clear **Active**.
1. Select **Save changes**.

An inactive user cannot sign in, and their API keys and MCP tokens stop working at once, not at the next sync. DAIV keeps their history and the runs they own.

### Delete a user

Delete a user only when you will never restore their access. Deactivating keeps their history and ownership of runs: see [Deactivate a user](#deactivate-a-user).

Deleting a user cannot be undone

Deleting removes the user's account, their API keys and all data associated with them. You cannot delete your own account.

1. Under **Admin** → **Users**, select the user.
1. Select **Delete user**.
1. On the confirmation page, select **Delete user**.

## Account pages

Every signed-in user, member or admin, has these pages. All but **Home** open from the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar.

| Page                      | Route                 | What it does                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Home**                  | `/dashboard/`         | Your landing page after sign-in, with a link to **Team insights**.                                                                                      |
| **API keys**              | `/accounts/api-keys/` | Create and revoke personal API keys for programmatic access.                                                                                            |
| **Notification channels** | `/accounts/channels/` | Choose how DAIV notifies you about your agent runs. [Notifications](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/notifications/index.md) lists the channels. |
| **Passkeys**              | `/accounts/mfa/`      | Add and remove the passkeys you sign in with.                                                                                                           |

API keys authenticate calls to the [Jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md) and the [MCP endpoint](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/mcp-endpoint/index.md). A member sees only their own keys, and an admin sees every user's keys in the list.

## Related pages

- **Deployment**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  Install DAIV, configure email, and create the first admin.

  [Deployment](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/getting-started/deployment/index.md)

- **Platform setup**

  Connect DAIV to GitLab or GitHub, the same platform used for OAuth login.

# LLM providers

DAIV runs on these LLM providers:

- [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) (default)
- [OpenAI](https://openai.com)
- [Anthropic](https://anthropic.com)
- [Google Gemini](https://gemini.google.com)

You can mix providers, for example OpenRouter for the main agent and a direct provider for one model override. An admin can add any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint as a [custom provider](#custom-providers).

## Provider API keys

DAIV reads a provider's API key once, at its first start, from the provider's environment variable or from a Docker secret named after the variable in lowercase, such as `openrouter_api_key`. From then on you change the keys, and the providers' other settings, under **Configuration** → **Providers** in the dashboard. A change to the variable or the secret after the first start has no effect.

[LLM providers](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#llm-providers) in the environment variables reference lists the variables. [Providers](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#providers) in the site configuration reference describes the fields of a provider.

## Set up a provider

Set up a provider before DAIV's first start. You need an API key from the provider, and the default models need only OpenRouter's key.

| Provider      | Get an API key                                             | Variable             |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| OpenRouter    | [OpenRouter Settings](https://openrouter.ai/settings/keys) | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| OpenAI        | [OpenAI](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys)             | `OPENAI_API_KEY`     |
| Anthropic     | [Anthropic](https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys)   | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`  |
| Google Gemini | [AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/apikey)            | `GOOGLE_API_KEY`     |

1. Get an API key from the provider's page in the table.
1. In DAIV's `.env` file, set the provider's variable to the key. Alternatively, mount a Docker secret named after the variable in lowercase.
1. Start DAIV.

A provider whose key was not set at the first start begins disabled. To set up a provider on a running install, open **Configuration** → **Providers**, set the provider's **API key**, turn on **Enabled**, and select **Save configuration**. Saving a key does not enable a disabled provider. [Providers](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#providers) describes the fields.

## Model specs

A model spec names a model and its provider. OpenRouter models take the `openrouter:` prefix. Direct providers' models take no prefix, and DAIV picks the provider from the start of the name:

| Provider               | Model spec                                                                                                                                           | Example                                  |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| OpenRouter             | `openrouter:` followed by the [model name from OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/models)                                                             | `openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` |
| Anthropic (direct)     | A name starting with `claude`, from the [model names Anthropic lists](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/all-models#model-names) | `claude-sonnet-5-5`                      |
| OpenAI (direct)        | A name starting with `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, `gpt-6` or `o4`, from the [model names OpenAI lists](https://platform.openai.com/docs/models)                 | `gpt-6.1-sol`                            |
| Google Gemini (direct) | A name starting with `gemini`, from the [model names Gemini lists](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models)                                     | `gemini-3.8-flash`                       |

A provider's slug also works as a prefix, so `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` is the same model as `claude-sonnet-5-5`. The slug of Google Gemini is `google_genai`, and DAIV also accepts `google:`.

To use a model spec for one repository, set it in `.daiv.yml`; [Model overrides](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#model-overrides) lists every option. For example:

```
models:
  agent:
    model: "claude-sonnet-5-5"
```

In the dashboard, the agent picker offers a model dropdown built from each enabled provider's API and cached for 15 minutes, so you can choose a model without typing its spec. Free-text entry stays available as a fallback.

## Default models

| Role             | Model                                    | Fallback                        |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Main agent       | `openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` | `openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol` |
| Max mode         | `openrouter:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5`   | The main agent's models         |
| Explore subagent | `openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5`  | The main agent's models         |

Smaller tasks such as titling, merge request metadata and memory have their own defaults, listed in [Environment variables](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/index.md). All defaults route through OpenRouter, so only `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is required for a basic setup. Choose the explore subagent's model with an `explore` entry in the subagent models: see [Subagents](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/subagents/#subagent-model-precedence).

## Retries on provider errors

DAIV retries a failed call to a provider's API when the failure is transient. For Anthropic's API, that means a connection error, or a 408, 409, 429 or 5xx response. DAIV retries up to `DAIV_MODEL_MAX_RETRIES` times (default `2`; see [Model requests](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#model-requests)). A 400 or 401 response is not retried. If the call still fails, DAIV tries the fallback model, when one is set. If that fails too, the run ends with the error.

If runs end on rate-limit errors, raise `DAIV_MODEL_MAX_RETRIES` or ask Anthropic for a higher rate limit.

## Custom providers

An admin can register providers beyond the four above, mainly self-hosted, OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM or an internal gateway. A custom provider works with any of the supported wire protocols.

You need the admin role to add a custom provider. Under **Configuration** → **Providers**, the steps in [Add a custom provider](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#add-a-custom-provider) create the provider with a slug, a provider type, a base URL, an API key and a few options. [Provider fields](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#provider-fields) describes them.

Once the provider exists, reference its models with the slug as a prefix:

```
<slug>:<model-name>
```

Replace `<slug>` with the provider's slug and `<model-name>` with a model the endpoint serves. You can use this prefix anywhere a model is specified, including the `.daiv.yml` [model overrides](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#model-overrides).

### Keep prompt caching on a self-hosted model

The agent loads most of its tools on demand. On models listed in `DEFERRED_TOOLS_FROZEN_TOOLS_MODELS`, loading a tool keeps the provider's prompt cache. On any other model, the first use of each tool re-sends the conversation uncached.

Before you add a self-hosted model to that list, check that it can call a tool it only saw in a `tool_search` result: run `tests/integration_tests/test_deferred_tools_frozen.py` against it, using the command in that file's docstring. List the model name without your provider slug, for example `qwen3-coder` for `vllm:qwen3-coder`. [Environment variables](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/index.md) describes the setting.
# Features

# Issue addressing

Issue addressing turns an issue into code. DAIV reads a labelled issue, posts an implementation plan, waits for your approval, and opens a merge request (GitLab) or pull request (GitHub) with the changes.

## How it works

1. You create or update an issue and add a bot label.
1. DAIV reads the issue title, description, and any attached images.
1. DAIV posts a plan as a comment on the issue.
1. You review the plan and approve it, or comment with the changes you want, and DAIV revises the plan.
1. DAIV implements the plan and opens a merge or pull request.

```
graph TD
    A["Create issue with daiv label"] --> B["DAIV analyzes issue"]
    B --> C["Plan posted as comment"]
    C --> D{"Approve?"}
    D -- "@daiv proceed" --> E["DAIV implements changes"]
    D -- "Comment with changes" --> B
    E --> F["Merge/Pull request created"]
```

## Issue labels

Add one of these bot labels to an issue to hand it to DAIV:

| Label       | Behavior                                                                   |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `daiv`      | Generates a plan and waits for approval before implementing                |
| `daiv-auto` | Generates a plan and executes it immediately without waiting for approval  |
| `daiv-max`  | Uses a more capable model with deeper reasoning; see [Max mode](#max-mode) |

Labels are case-insensitive (`DAIV`, `Daiv`, and `daiv` all work). You can combine labels: `daiv-auto` with `daiv-max` runs the plan at once, on the more capable model.

When the merge request DAIV opened for an issue merges, DAIV [archives the issue's session](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/#archived-sessions). A label or mention on the issue then starts nothing until someone unarchives the session, and DAIV replies with a link to it.

## Approve a plan

With the `daiv` label, DAIV waits for your approval after it posts a plan and makes no code changes before it. To approve the plan:

1. Open the issue and read the plan DAIV posted.

1. Add a comment that mentions DAIV, for example:

   ```
   @daiv proceed
   ```

The exact wording is not a keyword. DAIV reacts to any comment that mentions it (`@daiv`); it reads your comment together with the plan it posted and acts on your intent. A comment like `@daiv looks good, go ahead` works the same as `@daiv proceed`.

Your comment can also carry feedback or extra instructions. DAIV either applies them while it implements the plan or revises the plan from them. If you disagree with the plan, comment with the changes you want and DAIV updates the plan.

## Answer a question from DAIV

When the issue or your feedback is ambiguous in a way that changes the work, or the choice is yours to make, DAIV can post a question instead of guessing. The question mentions you and ends with "reply mentioning `@daiv` with your answer." To answer, leave a new comment that mentions DAIV. On GitLab, DAIV posts its question inside the discussion thread of the comment that triggered it, so replying in that same thread keeps the conversation together; on GitHub the question is always a top-level comment.

## Max mode

The `daiv-max` label switches DAIV to the site's max model with its max thinking level, which suits complex issues that need deeper analysis. An administrator sets both, with the `DAIV_AGENT_MAX_MODEL_NAME` and `DAIV_AGENT_MAX_THINKING_LEVEL` variables or in [Site configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/index.md); the [environment variables reference](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/index.md) lists their defaults.

## Run DAIV again

To run a second plan on an issue DAIV already addressed, add a new comment that mentions `@daiv` and says what you want. DAIV updates the existing merge or pull request instead of creating a new one. Adding the label again does not start a run: DAIV ignores a label on an issue it already reacted to.

## When a run fails

If an unexpected error stops DAIV while it implements a plan, DAIV opens a **draft** merge or pull request to keep the changes it already made.

## AGENTS.md suggestion

When DAIV creates a merge request for a repository that doesn't have an [`AGENTS.md`](https://agents.md/) file (or whatever `context_file_name` is configured to), DAIV adds a comment suggesting you create one. The comment includes a one-click link that opens an issue with the `daiv-auto` label already set. When you submit that issue, DAIV runs the [`/init` skill](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/#init) at once, with no approval step, and opens a merge or pull request with the generated `AGENTS.md`.

To stop the suggestion on one repository, set `suggest_context_file: false` in its `.daiv.yml`. To stop it on every repository, set `DAIV_SUGGEST_CONTEXT_FILE_ENABLED` to `false`. [Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/index.md) and the [environment variables reference](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/index.md) describe both.

## Turn off issue addressing

Issue addressing is on by default. To turn it off for a repository, add this to its `.daiv.yml`:

```
issue_addressing:
  enabled: false
```

[Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/index.md) lists every feature toggle and who can trigger DAIV.

## Related pages

- [Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/index.md) — restrict who can trigger DAIV and turn features on or off
- [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/index.md) — steer an issue with `/plan` and custom skills
- [Pull request assistant](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pull-request-assistant/index.md) — what happens once the merge request is open
- [Sandbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox/index.md) — where the implementation is built and tested

# Pull request assistant

The pull request assistant answers when you mention DAIV in a comment on a GitLab merge request or a GitHub pull request. DAIV applies review feedback, answers questions about the change, and fixes failing pipelines. The `/code-review` skill adds a full review: DAIV posts its findings as one [review report](#review-reports).

On GitLab this works on merge requests, on GitHub on pull requests. This page says "pull request" for both.

## Ask DAIV on a merge request

To ask DAIV for something on a pull request:

1. Open the pull request.

1. Add a comment that mentions DAIV:

   ```
   @daiv <your request>
   ```

   Replace `daiv` with your DAIV bot's username if it differs, and `<your request>` with what you want.

DAIV reacts to your comment with an eyes emoji to confirm it received the request, then replies or pushes changes to the branch.

### Where to comment

You can mention DAIV in two places:

- **Inline on the diff** — comment directly on specific lines of code. This reaches DAIV only on a merge request a DAIV session owns (see [A merge request DAIV published](#a-merge-request-daiv-published))
- **General discussion** — comment in the pull request conversation

DAIV sees the diff and the comment's position, so an inline comment tells it exactly what you mean.

### A merge request DAIV published

When a DAIV session published the merge or pull request, a mention goes to that session instead of starting a new one: the session that owns it (see [The session inbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/#the-session-inbox)). It picks up where the session left off, and acts as you: as the DAIV account you signed in to with that GitLab/GitHub account, with its personal MCP servers, never as the session's owner. If you never signed in to DAIV with that account, the run gets no personal tools, even when a DAIV user shares your username. Its final message, or its question, is posted in the thread of your mention; when you mentioned DAIV in several threads before it answered, the full reply goes in the latest one, and each other thread gets a line linking to it.

A mention on a diff line reaches DAIV only on a merge request a session owns. On GitHub this also needs the App subscribed to **Pull request review comment** (see [Platform setup](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/getting-started/platform-setup/#github-app-permissions-and-events)). Comments that don't mention DAIV aren't answered, but the owning session remembers them, and its next run sees them. It remembers them from anyone but DAIV itself, even from people left out of [`allowed_usernames`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#access-control); only a mention needs its author on that list.

## What DAIV can do

### Apply code changes

Ask DAIV to modify code based on your review feedback:

```
@daiv use Redis instead of in-memory storage
```

```
@daiv add error handling for the case when the API returns null
```

```
@daiv move this logic to a separate helper function
```

### Answer questions

Ask DAIV about the code to help you make review decisions:

```
@daiv why is this import inside the method instead of at the top?
```

```
@daiv is this approach thread-safe?
```

### Fix failing pipelines

When CI/CD fails, ask DAIV to investigate and fix it:

```
@daiv the pipeline is failing, can you fix it?
```

DAIV inspects the pipeline logs, identifies the root cause, and pushes a fix to the branch.

### Answer a question from DAIV

When your request is ambiguous in a way that changes the work, or the choice is yours to make, DAIV can post a question instead of guessing. The question mentions you and ends with "reply mentioning `@daiv` with your answer." To answer, leave a new comment that mentions DAIV. On GitLab, DAIV posts its question inside the discussion thread of the comment that triggered it, so replying in that same thread keeps the conversation together; on GitHub the question is a top-level comment, unless you asked on a diff line of a merge request a session owns, where it is posted in that thread.

## Conversation continuity

DAIV keeps its context across the mentions on one pull request. Each new mention builds on the earlier ones, so DAIV knows the history of changes and discussion. If DAIV drifts or gets stuck, comment `@daiv /clear` to reset the conversation; see [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/#clear).

## Review reports

DAIV posts each review as a single comment on the pull request — findings grouped by severity (Critical / Important / Suggestions), open questions for the author, and, when there are Critical or Important findings, a short list of recommended actions. On GitLab, reviews **stack**: a re-review posts a new report covering only the commits since the previous one (after a force-push, the next report covers the full change again and says so). If a review could not cover one of its dimensions — say the security detector failed — the report says so, and the next review re-covers that span rather than treating it as done. A review requested when nothing has changed since the last one answers with a one-line "already reviewed" note instead of a fresh report.

On GitHub the report carries no tracking marker: re-review scope comes from the conversation history on the pull request rather than from the reports themselves, so it is lost if that conversation is cleared — after which the next report covers the whole pull request again.

To ask about a finding or have DAIV apply a fix, reply on the pull request and mention DAIV.

## Custom review rules

Define team-specific review rules in `.agents/review-rules.md` at the repository root. Write them in plain language, one rule per bullet, with any path scope expressed in prose:

- *Every external API call in `src/payments/**` must set an explicit timeout.*
- *Never log request or response bodies.*
- *New Celery tasks must be idempotent.*

The code review agent checks for rule sources at the start of every review and, when any exist, runs a dedicated `cr-custom-rules` detector against the diff; each violation it posts cites the rule it enforces.

`.agents/review-rules.md` is optional: rules already written in your repository's `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/AGENTS.md` are a **secondary** source, which the agent mines for concrete conventions it can check against the diff. When sources disagree, `.agents/review-rules.md` wins. The detector is skipped only when none of these files exist.

Every custom-rule finding passes the same confidence gate and skeptical aggregation as built-in findings, so a noisy `AGENTS.md` does not flood the review.

## Turn off the assistant

The pull request assistant is on by default. To turn it off for a repository, add this to its `.daiv.yml`:

```
pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: false
```

[Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/index.md) lists every feature toggle.

## Related pages

- [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/index.md) — invoke `/code-review` from a merge request, and write custom skills to extend it
- [Sandbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox/index.md) — the isolated container where DAIV reproduces and repairs failing pipelines
- [Sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/index.md) — follow a running review and revisit what the agent changed
- [Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/index.md) — tune review behaviour per repository with `.daiv.yml`

# Pipeline watch

After DAIV publishes a merge request, it watches the merge request's CI and tells the session that published it what happened. A CI failure on a commit DAIV pushed wakes that session, up to a configurable number of times, to look at the failure and fix it; if the failure is not something a code change can fix, the run explains why instead of pushing. Everything else CI reports, a pass or a pipeline that needs a person, is remembered by the session and shown to the agent the next time it runs.

## Turn on CI events

Pipeline watch reacts to CI events, and each platform delivers them differently. Without these events, DAIV hears of CI only through the reconciler's poll, which re-reads a watched merge request that nothing was heard of for 30 minutes, so a failure can wait 30 minutes or more. On GitHub, DAIV also cannot read CI at all until the App's **Actions** permission is **Read-only**.

### GitLab

DAIV registers `pipeline_events` on a repository's webhook when it creates the webhook. To add the event to webhooks DAIV registered earlier, run this on the host that runs DAIV:

```
docker compose exec app django-admin setup_webhooks --update
```

[`setup_webhooks`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/management-commands/#setup_webhooks) describes the command.

### GitHub

`setup_webhooks` does nothing on GitHub, because a GitHub App's event subscriptions are central, not per repository. Subscribing the App covers every repository it is installed on:

1. Open your GitHub App's settings page and select **Permissions & events**.
1. Under **Repository permissions**, set **Actions** to **Read-only**. This permission lets the App subscribe to **Workflow run** and read job logs.
1. Under **Subscribe to events**, select **Workflow run**.
1. Select **Save changes**.
1. If **Actions** is a new permission for the App, ask each installation owner to accept it, from GitHub's email or the installation's **Configure** page. Pipeline watch stays off on an installation until its owner accepts.
1. After the next workflow run, open **Advanced** → **Recent Deliveries** and check for a `workflow_run` delivery.

[Platform setup](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/getting-started/platform-setup/#github-app-permissions-and-events) lists every event the App needs.

______________________________________________________________________

## How it works

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as DAIV Agent
    participant Session as Publishing session
    participant Watch as Pipeline Watch
    participant CI as GitLab / GitHub CI

    Agent->>Session: publish (records the pushed commit)
    CI-->>Watch: pipeline event (terminal state)
    Watch->>Watch: judge the head pipeline
    alt green
        Watch->>Session: CI passed (remembered)
    else needs a person (blocked / manual / canceled / skipped)
        Watch->>Session: CI stopped (remembered)
    else failure
        Watch->>Session: CI failed (wakes it, or remembered with a reason)
        Session->>Agent: run with the failed jobs and the pipeline link
        Agent->>CI: push a fix, or explain and push nothing
    end
```

The steps below give the same flow in text.

1. **The publishing session owns the merge request.** When a run publishes, its session claims the merge request and records the commit DAIV pushed. A later publish from another session of the same person moves the merge request to that session; a publish from another person's session leaves it where it is and tells the owning session. [Which runs claim a merge request](#which-runs-claim-a-merge-request) lists the cases.

1. **Pipeline event.** A webhook from GitLab (`pipeline_events`) or GitHub (`workflow_run`) delivers the terminal result. CI is also judged right after a publish, because the event can arrive before the claim exists. Only the merge request's head pipeline is judged; a pipeline an older push started is ignored.

1. **Judgment.** See [Conservative judgment](#conservative-judgment) below.

1. **Waking the session.** A failure wakes the owning session only when all of these hold. The first one that does not is recorded as the reason the failure was only remembered, and the agent sees it the next time it runs.

   | Condition                                                                                                                                                               | Reason when it fails   |
   | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
   | The watch is on for the repository and for this merge request                                                                                                           | Watch off              |
   | The pipeline ran on the commit DAIV last pushed                                                                                                                         | Not DAIV's commit      |
   | No CI run looked at that commit yet                                                                                                                                     | Already examined       |
   | Attempts are left                                                                                                                                                       | Attempts spent         |
   | DAIV has not started three runs in a row on the session without a person (see [The session inbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/#the-session-inbox)) | Too many runs in a row |

1. **The CI run.** DAIV runs it in the publishing session, on the merge request's branch, with a prompt naming the failed jobs and the pipeline URL. The agent reads the job logs through its `gitlab` / `gh` platform tool, then pushes a fix or explains why it pushed nothing. It can't ask a question: nobody is there to answer. If the session is busy, the failure waits and joins the session's next run.

1. **A run that pushes nothing** explains, without giving up. No push means no new pipeline, so the session shows CI as failing with a link to that run's explanation, and you receive its summary as a run notification. Retrying the same pipeline by hand does not wake the session again: the commit was already examined. If the retry passes, the session shows CI passing.

1. **Attempts spent.** When a failure on a new DAIV commit finds no attempts left, the merge request's owner is notified once for that commit. A run a person starts that publishes to the merge request gives the attempts back.

1. **Reconciler.** A cron task runs every 10 minutes and re-reads the CI of each watched merge request nothing was heard of for 30 minutes, whatever it last reported, so a missed webhook (a manual retry's, say) is repaired. On GitLab it reads the branch's latest pipeline; on GitHub, the latest run of each workflow on the branch's head commit. A pipeline already judged in its status is skipped without reading its jobs. Nothing expires: the watch observes until the merge request is merged or closed. Each tick re-reads at most 200 branches, the longest-quiet first, and a branch it could not read is tried again on the next tick.

______________________________________________________________________

## Conservative judgment

DAIV errs toward remembering rather than spending an attempt on something it cannot fix. The decision table:

Rows are evaluated top to bottom; the first match wins.

| Pipeline state                                                                            | Jobs                                                 | Outcome                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| still in progress (`created`, `pending`, `running`, `preparing`, …), or no pipeline found | any                                                  | **Not judged** — nothing posted; the next event or the reconciler looks again |
| `skipped`                                                                                 | zero jobs                                            | **Not judged** — a `ci.skip` push records this in place of a pipeline         |
| `blocked`, `manual`, `canceled`, `skipped`                                                | any                                                  | **Stopped** — remembered, shown as needing a person                           |
| any                                                                                       | zero jobs                                            | **Stopped** — remembered, shown as needing a person                           |
| `failed`                                                                                  | at least one non-`allow_failure` failed job          | **Failed** — may wake the session                                             |
| `failed`                                                                                  | no job reports `failed` at all (e.g. a config error) | **Failed** — may wake the session                                             |
| `failed`                                                                                  | every failed job is `allow_failure`                  | **Passed** — effectively a pass                                               |
| `success`                                                                                 | at least one job                                     | **Passed**                                                                    |

**Why zero-job pipelines are stopped, not passed:** a GitLab `.gitlab-ci.yml` that includes a cross-project template from a private repository resolves as the pushing identity. An ephemeral project-scoped token cannot read that private repository, so GitLab produces a pipeline with no jobs. Treating it as green would let a misconfigured pipeline pass silently; treating it as a failure would burn every attempt on a pipeline that was never going to run.

**Why blocked/manual/skipped/canceled are stopped:** these states reflect a human decision or an external gate. DAIV does not know whether to wait or act, so it remembers the result and lets you decide.

______________________________________________________________________

## CI status on the session page

The sidebar's repository cards show CI for each open merge request the session owns. A card shows **Waiting for CI** while no result has arrived since DAIV last pushed or while a run is looking at a failure. It then shows **Passing**, **Failing** or **Needs a person**. A failing merge request links the last run that looked at a failure, whose summary says what it found.

## Turn the watch on or off for a merge request

The **Fix CI failures** switch turns the watch on or off for one merge request. With it off, DAIV still remembers CI results but never wakes the session. Turning it on gives the merge request its attempts back and judges the branch's latest pipelines again at once (on GitHub, every workflow's), so a failure reported while the watch was off, or while no attempts were left, wakes the session. A commit a run already looked at is not looked at again. You need to be able to run agents on the repository.

1. Open the session that owns the merge request.
1. In the repository card, open the **⋯** menu.
1. Select **Fix CI failures**. A check mark shows the watch is on.

______________________________________________________________________

## Notifications

Every CI run produces the usual run notification, with the run's summary, so you hear what it found whether it pushed a fix or explained why it didn't. When attempts run out on a new DAIV commit, the merge request's owner gets one **CI still failing** notification for that commit, linking the owning session. A merge request whose owning session has no DAIV user behind it gets that outcome, and each CI run's summary, as a merge request comment instead.

______________________________________________________________________

## Limit or turn off pipeline watch

An administrator sets the site-wide switch and attempt cap under **Configuration** → **Pipeline Watch**, or with `DAIV_PIPELINE_WATCH_ENABLED` and `DAIV_PIPELINE_WATCH_MAX_ATTEMPTS`. With the switch off, no CI failure wakes a session, and sessions remember each failure with the reason *Watch off*. By default a merge request gets 3 fix attempts. [Site configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/index.md) and the [environment variables reference](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/index.md) describe both settings.

A repository can only tighten the site-wide values. Set its options in `.daiv.yml`:

```
pipeline_watch:
  enabled: true
  max_attempts: 2
```

`enabled: false` stops CI failures on the repository from waking a session. `max_attempts` is capped at the site-wide value, and `enabled: true` does not turn the watch on where the site turned it off. [Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#feature-toggles) lists both options.

______________________________________________________________________

## Platform notes

### GitHub: `allow_failure` jobs

The GitHub Actions API does not say which jobs are required, so DAIV treats every failed job as required. The verdict itself still comes from the workflow run's own conclusion, so a tolerated job's failure cannot by itself spend an attempt — a run that concludes `success` is green. What differs from GitLab is narrower: DAIV cannot exclude a tolerated job from the failure list it hands the agent, and it never reads a failed run as green on the grounds that every failure was tolerated.

### GitHub: one event per workflow, not per push

A `workflow_run` event reports a single workflow, not the branch's whole CI. A repository with several workflows on one push delivers one event per workflow, each judged on its own — so the first workflow to finish green can show CI as passing while another is still running or about to fail. Repositories that split required checks across workflows should expect the status to flip as each workflow reports. A session that delegated the work is told its CI passed only once the latest run of every workflow on the commit has passed.

### GitLab: child pipelines

A child pipeline (`trigger: include:`) runs on its parent's branch and commit, so DAIV ignores it and judges the parent pipeline, which is the merge request's result. For a child's failure to count, trigger it with `strategy: depend`, so the parent pipeline fails with it.

### GitLab: merge-request pipelines and the reconciler poll

The reconciler's fallback poll lists pipelines by branch (`ref=<source branch>`). Detached merge-request pipelines are not on the branch ref — GitLab records them under `refs/merge-requests/<iid>/head` — so on projects that run *only* merge-request pipelines the poll finds nothing. This is harmless: a read that finds no pipeline posts nothing, so those repositories are driven entirely by the pipeline webhook.

______________________________________________________________________

## Which runs claim a merge request

| How the merge request was published                                                  | Session that owns it                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Issue addressing (`daiv`, `daiv-auto` or `daiv-max` label, or a mention on an issue) | The issue's session                                 |
| Job runs — REST API, MCP `submit_job`, scheduled jobs                                | The job's session                                   |
| Chat turn                                                                            | The chat session                                    |
| A CI run in the owning session                                                       | Stays with that session, keeping the attempts spent |
| Review addressing (DAIV answering comments on a merge request no session owns)       | **None**                                            |

Review addressing is excluded deliberately. It pushes to a merge request someone else may own, so babysitting that pipeline would put commits nobody asked for on their branch. Reviewers who want CI fixed can ask for it in a comment.

______________________________________________________________________

## What pipeline watch does not do

- **Watches only merge requests DAIV published.** There is no opt-in label to watch an existing merge request.
- **Does not distinguish flaky from real failures.** Every failure on DAIV's commit may wake the session; the attempt cap bounds the cost, and a run that finds nothing to fix says so.
- **Does not react to CI on the default branch.** The watch is scoped to the merge request's branch.

______________________________________________________________________
