Runs that webhooks start, such as [issue addressing](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/index.md) and the [pull request assistant](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pull-request-assistant/index.md), report back in the issue or request thread. Like runs you start from the dashboard, the [jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md) or the [MCP endpoint](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/mcp-endpoint/index.md), they also notify their initiator when the outcome notifies. To silence a run you start through the API or MCP, pass the `muted` flag.

These events cover runs and schedules:

| Event                                               | When it fires                                                                                                                                                                                     | Recipients                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Job finished** (`job.finished`)                   | A single agent run finishes with an outcome that notifies.                                                                                                                                        | The user who started the run.                                                                                                   |
| **Job batch finished** (`job_batch.finished`)       | Every run in a multi-run batch has finished. DAIV sends one rollup, not one message per run.                                                                                                      | The batch owner and, for a [scheduled](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/scheduled-jobs/index.md) batch, its subscribers. |
| **Schedule finished** (`schedule.finished`)         | A run of a [scheduled job](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/scheduled-jobs/index.md) finishes with an outcome that notifies.                                                               | The schedule's owner and subscribers.                                                                                           |
| **Schedule can't run** (`schedule_dispatch.failed`) | A [scheduled job](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/scheduled-jobs/#when-a-schedule-cant-run) fails to start a run. DAIV sends it once per failing streak, even when the schedule is muted. | The schedule's owner.                                                                                                           |

A batch is a group of runs that share a batch ID, for example a scheduled job that fans out across several repositories. For a multi-run batch, DAIV suppresses the per-run notifications and sends one **Job batch finished** rollup once the last run has finished. The rollup says how many runs notified and how many were all-clear. A run waiting for an answer counts as notifying, and the rollup lists it right after the failures.

Other notifications, such as the one DAIV sends when [pipeline watch](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pipeline-watch/#notifications) runs out of attempts, are described with their features.

## Channels

DAIV reaches you through channels. In-app notifications are always on. Email, Rocket.Chat and Telegram are external channels, and your administrator decides which of the last two appear.

| Channel         | What you get                                                                                                         | What it needs                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| In-app          | **Notifications** in the sidebar shows your unread count and opens your full history at `/dashboard/notifications/`. | Nothing.                                                                                                        |
| Email           | A message to your account email address.                                                                             | Nothing. DAIV keeps a verified email channel in sync with your account address, so there is nothing to connect. |
| **Rocket Chat** | A direct message from the DAIV bot.                                                                                  | An administrator has enabled Rocket.Chat, and you have connected your `@username`.                              |
| **Telegram**    | A direct message from the DAIV bot.                                                                                  | An administrator has enabled Telegram, and you have connected your chat.                                        |

A message about a run includes the run's summary. For a run waiting for an answer, that is the list of questions.

### The in-app list

DAIV writes an in-app entry for each run whose outcome notifies, and none for an all-clear run.

- `/dashboard/notifications/` lists your full history. Filter it with **All**, **Unread** and **Read**, or select **Mark all as read**. Opening a notification marks it read. The **Settings** link opens your [notification channels](#connect-a-channel).
- The unread badge next to **Notifications** and the session lists in the sidebar update live over a server-sent events stream (`GET /api/nav/events`), so a new notification or a run starting or finishing appears without a reload. The stream needs Redis. Without it, they show their values from when the page loaded.

## Connect a channel

Email and in-app need no setup. Rocket.Chat and Telegram need an administrator to enable them first, and you then connect your own account on the channels page.

You need:

- For Rocket.Chat, an administrator who has enabled it in **Settings** → **Configuration** → **Rocket Chat**, with the instance URL, bot user ID and auth token. See [Site configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#setting-groups).
- For Telegram, an administrator who has enabled it in **Settings** → **Configuration** → **Telegram**, as described in [Set up Telegram](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/#set-up-telegram). Telegram delivery to chats that are already linked needs only outbound internet access, but connecting a new chat needs DAIV reachable from the internet over HTTPS. On an instance without public ingress, you cannot link new chats.
- Until the channel is enabled, its row does not appear on your channels page.

To open the channels page, select **Notification channels** in the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar (`/accounts/channels/`).

### Connect Rocket.Chat

1. On the **Notification channels** page, find the **Rocket Chat** row.
1. Enter your Rocket.Chat `@username`. DAIV strips a leading `@`.
1. Select **Connect**.

DAIV checks the username against the Rocket.Chat instance. On success, the row shows a **Verified** badge and your handle. If the user is unknown or the instance is unreachable, DAIV shows an error and saves nothing: it stores no unverified binding.

To stop Rocket.Chat delivery, select **Disconnect** in the same row.

### Connect Telegram

A Telegram bot cannot start a conversation with you, so connecting is a handshake: you message the bot first, through a single-use link that DAIV gives you.

Warning

The link links whichever Telegram chat opens it first to your DAIV account. Do not forward it or share it.

1. On the **Notification channels** page, find the **Telegram** row.
1. Select **Connect**. DAIV hands you off to Telegram.
1. In Telegram, open the chat with the DAIV bot. Telegram sends `/start` for you.
1. Read the bot's reply, which confirms the connection, and check that the row on your channels page shows **Verified** and your Telegram handle.

You have nothing else to confirm, because messaging the bot is the verification.

The link works for 10 minutes and stops working as soon as any chat is linked to your account. If it expires, the bot tells you, and you start again from the channels page. If the row shows `Not ready — ask an administrator to finish the Telegram setup.` instead of **Connect**, ask your administrator to finish the setup.

A few rules apply to the link:

- DAIV keeps at most one Telegram chat per account and one account per chat. Connecting from a different Telegram account replaces the previous link, and `/start` from a chat that is linked elsewhere moves it to you.
- The bot links only one-to-one chats. If you add it to a group and send `/start` there, it replies `Message me directly — DAIV notifications are per-account and cannot go to a group.` and links nothing.

To stop Telegram delivery, do any one of these: select **Disconnect** on your channels page, send `/stop` to the bot, or block the bot in Telegram. Each unlinks the chat, and the row goes back to **Not configured**; select **Connect** to link again.

If DAIV could not be told that you blocked the bot, for example because its webhook was unreachable or Telegram refused the chat for another reason, the link stays on the row marked **Unverified** and delivers nothing. Select **Connect** to redo the handshake. If that does not clear it, select **Disconnect**, then **Connect**.

## Muting

Notifications fire on outcomes that notify, and you have no per-outcome setting. The only control is muting:

- **Scheduled runs.** A schedule's **Mute notifications** setting, off by default, silences every notification for that schedule's runs: no in-app entry and no external delivery. It does not silence **Schedule can't run**, which reports that the schedule did not run at all. Muting applies to the owner and every subscriber alike.
- **Other runs.** Runs you start from the dashboard, the [jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md) or the [MCP endpoint](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/mcp-endpoint/index.md) notify you on an outcome that notifies. Pass the `muted` flag in the API or MCP call to silence a run.

A muted run produces no in-app entry at all: muting is full silence. DAIV has no setting for turning email off while keeping in-app notifications.

## How delivery works

When a run finishes with an outcome that notifies, DAIV records the notification, then one delivery for each external channel, and sends each delivery from a background worker:

- A channel with no usable connection, such as Rocket.Chat or Telegram before you connect, or a channel DAIV does not know, is recorded as **skipped** rather than attempted.
- DAIV retries a transient failure, up to three attempts in all, waiting 1 minute before the second and 5 minutes before the third. A permanent failure, such as a refused recipient or a disabled channel, is marked **failed** and not retried. When the provider names its own wait, as Telegram's flood control does, DAIV delays the next attempt to at least that long, up to one hour.
- Blocking the DAIV bot in Telegram normally unlinks your chat at once. When that message does not reach DAIV, DAIV notices the refusal on the next delivery instead. It keeps the link and marks it **Unverified**, because that condition never recovers by itself and retrying would only use up attempts. Later notifications are **skipped**, until you redo the handshake.
- The in-app entry does not depend on external delivery. DAIV writes it even when every external channel is skipped or fails.

## Related pages

- [Scheduled jobs](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/scheduled-jobs/index.md): recurring runs with a mute setting and a subscriber list.
- [Jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md): submit runs programmatically, with a `muted` flag.
- [Sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/index.md): every notification links to its session or batch in the sessions list.
- [MCP endpoint](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/mcp-endpoint/index.md): submit jobs from MCP clients, with a `muted` flag.

# Merge metrics

DAIV records every merge request (GitLab) or pull request (GitHub) merged into a default branch. For each merge it counts the lines changed and attributes them to DAIV or to people, commit by commit. The dashboard's **Insights** page shows the totals as code velocity.

______________________________________________________________________

## How it works

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Platform as GitLab / GitHub
    participant DAIV as DAIV
    participant Dashboard as Insights page

    Platform->>DAIV: merge event
    DAIV->>DAIV: skip unless the target is the default branch
    DAIV->>Platform: fetch diff statistics and the commit list
    DAIV->>DAIV: attribute each commit by author email
    Dashboard->>DAIV: read the totals for the chosen period
```

The steps below give the same flow in text.

1. **DAIV receives a merge event.** GitLab sends a `merge_request` webhook with `action: merge`; GitHub sends a `pull_request` webhook with `action: closed` and `merged: true`.
1. **DAIV checks the target branch.** It records only merges into the repository's default branch, and ignores merges into feature or release branches.
1. **DAIV fetches the data.** A background task fetches the merge's diff statistics and its commit list from the platform API.
1. **DAIV attributes the lines.** It compares each commit's author email with DAIV's bot commit email, and splits the lines added and removed into DAIV's and people's.
1. **DAIV shows the totals.** The **Code velocity** section of the **Insights** page uses the same period filter as the agent activity counters: **Today**, **7 days**, **30 days**, **90 days** or **All time**, with **7 days** as the default.

If a platform call fails, DAIV still records the merge. When only the diff statistics fail, DAIV takes the lines changed from the sum over the commits; a figure whose own fetch failed stays at zero.

______________________________________________________________________

## Code velocity metrics

Everyone sees the **Code velocity** section, counted over the repositories they can read (administrators: every repository). It stays hidden when the period has no merges. The period filter at the top of the page applies to every figure.

| Figure on the page     | What it counts                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **merges**             | Merge and pull requests merged into default branches                                                                                                     |
| **involved DAIV**      | The share of merges with at least one DAIV-authored commit, with both counts                                                                             |
| **of commits by DAIV** | The share of commits authored by DAIV, with both counts                                                                                                  |
| **lines changed**      | Lines added and removed across all merges                                                                                                                |
| **Merges over time**   | Merges per day (per week for 30 and 90 days, per month for all time), split into those that involved DAIV and those by people only. Hidden for **Today** |

______________________________________________________________________

## Attribution

DAIV identifies its own commits by matching the commit author email against its bot email:

- **GitLab:** the bot user's `commit_email`, else its `public_email`, else its `email`, else `<username>@users.noreply.gitlab.com`
- **GitHub:** `<user_id>+<app_slug>[bot]@users.noreply.github.com`

### Mixed authorship

A merge request can hold commits from both DAIV and people. When a person opens one and then asks DAIV for follow-up changes with `@daiv`, DAIV splits the lines by each commit's author.

### Commit limits

On GitLab, DAIV attributes the first 100 commits of a merge request. On GitHub, the platform lists at most 250 commits per pull request.

### Squash merges

A squash merge collapses the commits into one on the target branch, but the platform API keeps the original commit list. DAIV attributes lines from that list, so squash merges are attributed like any other.

______________________________________________________________________

## Turn on merge metrics

Merge metrics need no configuration: DAIV records merges as soon as it receives merge events.

- **GitLab:** DAIV registers `merge_requests_events` on each repository's webhook when it creates it. To add the event to webhooks registered earlier, run `docker compose exec app django-admin setup_webhooks --update`; see [`setup_webhooks`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/management-commands/#setup_webhooks).
- **GitHub:** DAIV registers nothing. Subscribe your GitHub App to **Pull request**; [Platform setup](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/getting-started/platform-setup/#github-app-permissions-and-events) lists every event the App needs.

## Related pages

- [Sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/index.md) — the run history behind the DAIV-authored commits these metrics attribute
- [Issue addressing](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/index.md) — the workflow that produces most DAIV-authored merges

# Slash commands and skills

DAIV responds to slash commands in issue and merge or pull request comments, and some also work in the dashboard chat. Built-in commands have fixed behavior. **Skills** are packaged instructions that give DAIV expertise for a specific task. You invoke both the same way:

```
@daiv /<command> [arguments]
```

Use `/help` to list everything available where you are.

## Built-in commands

These commands have fixed behavior:

| Command   | Scopes                          | Description                                    |
| --------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `/help`   | Issues, MRs/PRs, dashboard chat | Lists all available commands and skills        |
| `/agents` | Issues, MRs/PRs, dashboard chat | Lists available subagents with descriptions    |
| `/clear`  | Issues, MRs/PRs                 | Resets the conversation context to start fresh |

### /help

```
@daiv /help
```

Lists the slash commands and skills available in the current scope: the built-in commands, and the built-in and custom skills of the repository.

### /agents

```
@daiv /agents
```

Lists the available subagents with their names and descriptions. See [Subagents](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/subagents/index.md) for details.

### /clear

```
@daiv /clear
```

Starts a fresh conversation context for the current issue or merge/pull request. Use it when DAIV's context is stale or DAIV starts drifting. The earlier conversation stays in the session's history; DAIV stops seeing it.

### In the dashboard chat

`/help` and `/agents` are also registered for the global scope, so they work in the dashboard chat too. Typing `/` in the chat composer opens a list of suggestions with those commands and the global skills. Per-repository skills do not appear there: they live in the repository's sandbox, which DAIV cannot read while the page renders.

## Built-in skills

DAIV ships with these built-in skills:

| Skill             | Description                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/plan`           | Explores the codebase in read-only mode and produces an implementation plan                                                              |
| `/code-review`    | Reviews a merge/pull request for correctness, security, performance, structure, changed tests, and your repository's custom review rules |
| `/security-audit` | Audits code for security vulnerabilities, injection flaws, hardcoded secrets, and risks                                                  |
| `/init`           | Analyzes the repository and generates or updates an `AGENTS.md` guidance file                                                            |
| `/skill-creator`  | Guides you through creating a new custom skill                                                                                           |

### /plan

```
@daiv /plan implement rate limiting for the API
```

DAIV explores the codebase without making any changes and posts a detailed implementation plan. DAIV runs it automatically when it addresses an issue without the `daiv-auto` label (see [Issue addressing](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/index.md)).

### /code-review

```
@daiv /code-review
```

Reviews the current merge/pull request diff for correctness, security, performance, structure, changed tests (when the diff touches test files), and your repository's [custom review rules](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pull-request-assistant/#custom-review-rules). Posts numbered findings grouped by severity, as a single report comment.

How it scores on the ReviewBench benchmark, and at what cost, is on the [Benchmarks](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/benchmarks/index.md) page.

### /security-audit

```
@daiv /security-audit
```

Performs a dedicated security scan of the code changes, looking for injection flaws, hardcoded secrets, authentication issues, and data handling risks.

### /init

```
@daiv /init
```

Analyzes the repository structure and generates an `AGENTS.md` file: short, repository-specific guidance for AI coding agents, covering verified commands, a repository map, invariants and pitfalls, and where changes usually go. If the file already exists, `/init` updates it to cut duplication and low-signal text.

### /skill-creator

```
@daiv /skill-creator
```

Walks you through creating a custom skill for your repository. See [Agent skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/agent-skills/index.md) for more on custom skills.

## Turn off slash commands

Slash commands are on by default. To turn them off for a repository, add this to its `.daiv.yml`:

```
slash_commands:
  enabled: false
```

[Repository configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#feature-toggles) lists every feature toggle.

## Create a custom command

A custom slash command is a skill: creating the skill registers the command, with no separate step. To create a command named `/my-command`:

1. Create `.agents/skills/my-command/SKILL.md`, starting with YAML frontmatter.
1. In a comment, invoke it with `@daiv /my-command`.

The command then appears in `/help` next to the built-in ones. [Agent skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/agent-skills/index.md) explains how to write a skill.

# Subagents

DAIV's main agent can delegate work to subagents. Each subagent is specialized for one kind of task: one explores the codebase quickly, another handles complex multi-step work. The main agent decides when to delegate, based on the task.

To see the subagents available in a repository, run [`/agents`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/#agents). It works in the dashboard chat and on any issue or merge or pull request. The list holds every available subagent: the two built-in subagents below, the code-review detectors, and any custom subagents the repository defines.

## Built-in subagents

### General-purpose

The general-purpose subagent researches complex questions, searches for code, and carries out multi-step tasks. It has the main agent's tools:

- Filesystem operations (read, search, edit)
- Git platform tools (GitLab or GitHub)
- Web search and fetch, when enabled
- Sandbox command execution, when the run has a [sandbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox/index.md)
- Task tracking
- The MCP tools the main agent has

The main agent delegates to it when a task needs several rounds of searching and reasoning, for example investigating a bug across several files or researching how an external library works before making changes.

### Explore

The explore subagent is a fast, read-only agent for navigating a codebase. Its tools list directories, read files, find files by glob pattern (for example `src/components/**/*.tsx`), and search code for keywords and regular expressions. It cannot modify files, run commands, or reach external resources, which keeps it fast and safe for quick lookups.

The main agent delegates to it to locate files, understand code structure, or gather context before deciding. The main agent gives it a thoroughness level: `quick`, `medium` or `very thorough`. Explore runs on `openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` unless a [configured model](#subagent-model-precedence) replaces it.

### Code-review detectors

The `/code-review` skill delegates to read-only detector subagents: `cr-correctness`, `cr-security`, `cr-performance`, `cr-structure`, `cr-tests` and `cr-custom-rules`. See [Subagent model precedence](#subagent-model-precedence) for the model they run on.

## How delegation works

The main agent chooses a subagent from the task:

- To find a file or understand code structure, it uses the explore subagent.
- To research, run commands, or do multi-step work, it uses the general-purpose subagent.
- To make code changes directly, it does the work itself.

Each subagent runs in its own isolated context. It does not see the main conversation and cannot exchange messages with the main agent. It works on its own and returns a single final report, which the main agent uses to continue the task.

## Add a custom subagent

A custom subagent is a Markdown file in the repository. You need write access to the repository.

1. In the repository root, create the directory `.agents/subagents/` if it does not exist.
1. In it, create one `.md` file for the subagent. The file name is free: the subagent's name comes from the file's `name` field.
1. Start the file with YAML frontmatter that sets `name` and `description`.
1. Optional: set `model` in the frontmatter to run the subagent on a model of your choice.
1. After the frontmatter, write the subagent's system prompt in Markdown.
1. Commit the file to the repository.
1. On the next run, send `/agents` to check that the subagent is listed.

```
my-repository/
├── .agents/
│   └── subagents/
│       ├── database-migration.md
│       └── data-analyst.md
└── src/
```

A subagent file looks like this:

```
---
name: database-migration
description: Specialized agent for planning and reviewing database migrations. Use when the task involves schema changes, data migrations, or ORM model modifications.
model: openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
---

You are a database migration specialist. When given a task:

1. Review the current schema by reading model files
2. Identify all affected tables and relationships
3. Plan the migration steps in order
4. Check for data loss risks
5. Suggest rollback strategies
```

A custom subagent has the same tools as the built-in [general-purpose subagent](#general-purpose).

## Custom subagent file format

DAIV reads the `.md` files directly inside `.agents/subagents/`, not those in subdirectories. It skips a file that breaks the rules below and logs a warning, and the subagent does not appear in `/agents`.

| Part          | Required | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`        | Yes      | The subagent's unique name, which the main agent uses to delegate. It cannot be `general-purpose`, `explore`, or a code-review detector's name such as `cr-security`: DAIV skips a file that uses one.                                                                                                        |
| `description` | Yes      | What the subagent does. The main agent reads it to decide when to delegate, so make it specific and include trigger phrases.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `model`       | No       | The model to run on, as `provider:model-name`, for example `openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5`. Without it, the subagent runs on the main agent's model. A [configured model](#subagent-model-precedence) takes precedence. If DAIV cannot build the model and none is configured, it skips the subagent. |
| Body          | Yes      | The Markdown after the frontmatter becomes the subagent's system prompt. An empty body makes DAIV skip the file.                                                                                                                                                                                              |

DAIV ignores any other frontmatter key.

## Write a subagent description

The `description` is how the main agent decides whether to delegate to your subagent. Include specific trigger phrases:

```
# Good: specific triggers the agent can match
description: >
  Specialized agent for API endpoint design and implementation.
  Use when the task involves creating new REST endpoints, modifying
  API responses, or designing request/response schemas.

# Bad: too vague
description: Helps with API stuff.
```

## Subagent model precedence

Operators can run any subagent on a chosen model by name, without editing its file: the general-purpose and explore subagents, each code-review detector, and custom subagents. A custom subagent's file lives in the repository, so the dashboard does not list it. Set its model in `.daiv.yml`, or for every repository in `DAIV_AGENT_SUBAGENT_MODELS`.

A subagent's model is the first of these that is set:

1. Its entry under `models.subagents` in the repository's `.daiv.yml` (see [Model overrides](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#skill-and-subagent-models)).
1. Its entry in the dashboard or in `DAIV_AGENT_SUBAGENT_MODELS`. For the general-purpose and explore subagents, it is under **Configuration** → **Agent** → **Subagent models**. For the detectors, it is on the **Models** tab of the `code-review` skill's page.
1. The `model` that its file or detector charter declares (`openrouter:anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` for explore).
1. The main agent's model.

A configured model runs with the run's thinking level and falls back to the main agent's fallback models. A model that the user picks for the run does not override an entry, and a skill's model never carries over to a subagent it delegates to.

When an entry names a provider that is unknown, disabled or missing its API key, the subagent runs on its file's `model`, else on the main agent's model, so it is never left out of the run. DAIV logs the failure at ERROR. When a call on the configured model fails, for example because the provider does not know the model name, the main agent's fallback models serve it, as for any other model.

## Related pages

- [Agent tools](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/agent-architecture/index.md): the tools the main agent has, and when each is on
- [Agent skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/agent-skills/index.md): author the reusable instruction packages the main agent loads from `.agents/skills/`
- [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/index.md): run `/agents` to list every subagent available in a repository

# Sandbox

The sandbox is the isolated runtime where DAIV's agent runs shell commands: tests, linters, dependency installs, build scripts and git inspection. [daiv-sandbox](https://github.com/srtab/daiv-sandbox/), a companion service, starts and manages it. The agent reaches it through the `bash` tool, and a command policy decides which commands it may run.

## What the agent can do

With a sandbox, the agent can:

- Run tests and linters to validate changes.
- Install and update dependencies (npm, pip, uv and others), which needs [network access](#prerequisites).
- Inspect git state (`git status`, `git diff`, `git log`).
- Execute build scripts and generators.
- Run any command that the [command policy](#command-policy) allows.

## Prerequisites

The agent runs commands only when it has a sandbox, and installs only when the sandbox has network access:

- **A base image.** A run has a sandbox only when its [sandbox environment](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox-environments/index.md) sets a base image. When no environment matches the run (none selected, none bound to the repository, and no global default), the run has no sandbox and the agent gets no `bash` tool. A fresh install seeds a global **Default** environment, so a fresh install starts with a sandbox. See [How an environment is resolved](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox-environments/#how-an-environment-is-resolved).
- **Network access for installs.** Installing or updating dependencies reaches package registries such as npm and PyPI. A sandbox has no outbound network access unless its environment has **Network** set to **On** and an egress policy that allows the registries, so these commands fail until you set both. See [Network access and egress policy](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox-environments/#network-access-and-egress-policy).

## Sandbox session lifetime

A sandbox session works on the repository's code and keeps its state between commands, so the agent can install a dependency in one step and use it in the next.

When a run ends, whether it finished, failed or stopped, DAIV stops the sandbox session. The next turn of the same session restarts it, so what the agent installed is still there. The turn starts from a fresh sandbox instead when the session's [environment changed](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox-environments/#change-an-environment) or the sandbox service no longer has the old one.

## Command timeouts

Each command times out after 5 minutes. The agent can give a command it expects to run longer, such as a full test suite or a build, a longer timeout, up to the sandbox timeout (`DAIV_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT`, see [Environment variables](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#sandbox-client-side)). A sandbox timeout below 5 minutes lowers the default too. A timed-out command ends with exit code `124`.

DAIV adds advice to the output of a timed-out command: run it again with a larger timeout when there is room, or narrow it down. With daiv-sandbox 0.5.0 a timed-out command can keep running in the sandbox, so DAIV also tells the agent to stop it before running it again.

## Command policy

Not every command is safe for an AI agent to run. DAIV checks each command against a command policy before it reaches the sandbox. A command DAIV cannot parse is blocked, and the agent gets the reason.

### Built-in rules

DAIV always blocks the following commands. No setting overrides them.

| Category                | Blocked commands                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Git history mutation    | `git commit`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git rebase`, `git merge` (except `git merge --no-commit --no-ff <ref>` with no flag that commits or fast-forwards, and `git merge --abort`), `git pull`, `git cherry-pick`, `git revert`, `git am`, `git reflog delete`, `git filter-branch`, `git filter-repo` |
| Branch switching        | `git checkout`, `git switch`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Git index manipulation  | `git add`, `git stage`, `git hash-object`, `git update-index`, `git read-tree`, `git commit-tree`                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Destructive operations  | `git clean`, `git restore .`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Branch and tag deletion | `git branch -D` and `git branch --delete`, `git tag -d` and `git tag --delete`                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Git configuration       | `git config`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Platform CLI tools      | `gitlab`, `gh`, `python -m gitlab`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

DAIV commits, pushes and manages branches through its own tools, so the sandbox is for everything else. DAIV pushes the branch the run started on, so the agent cannot switch branches and restores files with `git restore <path>` instead of `git checkout`.

The agent can still merge a branch in, for example to resolve a merge request's conflicts with its target branch. It runs `git merge --no-commit --no-ff <ref>` and resolves the conflicts, and DAIV commits the result as a merge commit at the end of the turn, listing the files that conflicted. If a conflicted file still contains conflict markers, DAIV commits and pushes nothing, and says so in its reply.

The policy checks every command in the invocation, including those in chains, pipelines, `if` and `case` statements, loops, subshells and functions. It looks past leading variable assignments, so `HUSKY=0 git commit` is blocked. It does not look inside command or process substitutions (`$(…)`, backticks, `<(…)`), variable expansions (`git $cmd`), `bash -c` or `eval` strings, or wrappers such as `env`, and it compares words exactly as written, so `/usr/bin/git push`, `\git push` and `git "push"` pass. It is a guardrail that stops the agent's plain invocations, not a security boundary.

### Global rules

An operator can block more commands with `DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW`, a JSON array such as `["curl", "npm publish"]`. See [Environment variables](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#sandbox-client-side) for the variable. Each entry is a command name followed by the arguments that must appear after it, in that order but not necessarily next to each other, so `npm publish` also blocks `npm run publish`.

- For `git`, the first argument must be the git subcommand itself: `git revert` blocks `git -C repo revert` but not `git log --grep revert`.
- When a git option the policy does not know comes before the subcommand, the rule matches its arguments anywhere, so an unfamiliar option cannot hide a blocked subcommand.
- Matching ignores case and the order of bundled short flags, so `rm -rf` also blocks `rm -fr`.

`DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_ALLOW` takes the same format and has no effect (see [Precedence](#precedence)).

The policy is global: there is no per-repository or per-environment policy. DAIV ignores a `sandbox.command_policy` section left in `.daiv.yml` from v2.0.0 without a warning, so move its `disallow` entries to `DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW`.

### Precedence

DAIV checks the rules in this order and stops at the first that applies:

1. **Built-in rules** always win and cannot be overridden.
1. **Configured disallow rules** from `DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_DISALLOW` cannot be overridden by an allow rule.
1. **Configured allow rules** from `DAIV_SANDBOX_COMMAND_POLICY_ALLOW` allow only what step 4 already allows, so they change nothing.
1. **Default**: every other command is allowed.

## Sandbox configuration

A sandbox environment holds a sandbox's base image, CPUs, memory, network access and environment variables, not `.daiv.yml`. See [Sandbox environments](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox-environments/index.md) to create one and to see how DAIV picks the environment for a run.

# Sandbox environments

A sandbox environment is a named, reusable [sandbox](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sandbox/index.md) runtime: a base image, CPU and memory limits, an egress policy, encrypted environment variables, and the repositories it applies to. You define it once, and DAIV reuses it for every run, chat, scheduled job, and API or MCP call that lands in a matching repository.

An environment is how you give the agent a toolchain image, outbound network access to install dependencies, or a secret such as an API token or a private registry credential. When no environment matches a run (none selected, none bound to the repository, and no global default), the run has no sandbox and the agent gets no `bash` tool.

To manage environments, select **Settings** → **Sandbox environments** in the sidebar (`/dashboard/sandbox-envs/`). **Settings** is the cog beside your account at the bottom of the sidebar. **Global environments** lists the shared environments, and **My environments** lists yours.

## Scopes

An environment has one of two scopes:

| Scope      | Who sees it | Who manages it |
| ---------- | ----------- | -------------- |
| **User**   | Only you    | You            |
| **Global** | Everyone    | Administrators |

Any signed-in user creates, changes and deletes their own User environments. Only administrators create, change and delete Global environments, and only they can make one the default. Other users see Global environments in the list and can select them for a run. In the form, the **Scope** choice offers only **Personal** to other users, and offers **Shared with everyone** (a Global environment) to administrators as well.

When DAIV picks an environment for a repository, a User environment that claims the repository wins over a Global one, so you can override an organization-wide setup for the repositories you care about.

### Global default

One Global environment can be the default. DAIV falls back to it when no other environment matches a repository, and it supplies the CPUs, memory and environment variables that other environments leave unset (see [How an environment is resolved](#how-an-environment-is-resolved)). A fresh install seeds a global environment named **Default** with a base image, set as the default. With no global default, a run that matches no environment has no sandbox.

To make an environment the global default, as an administrator:

Changing the default replaces sandboxes

The default's settings flow into the effective runtime of every session that inherits from it, so making another environment the default replaces those sessions' sandboxes on their next turn, and anything installed in them or left uncommitted is lost.

1. In **Global environments**, find the environment.
1. Select **Make default**. The environment gets a **default** tag, and the previous default loses it.

You cannot delete the global default: DAIV shows `Set another global environment as default before deleting this one.` Make another environment the default first.

## Create an environment

You need a base image for the environment, such as `python:3.14`. To let the agent install dependencies, you also need to know which hosts it must reach.

1. In the sidebar, select **Settings** → **Sandbox environments**.
1. Select **New environment**. The **New sandbox environment** drawer opens.
1. Fill in the fields in the table below, starting with **Name** and **Base image**.
1. Select **Save**. The drawer closes, and the environment appears in its list.

| Field                     | What to enter                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Name**                  | A label of up to 80 characters, unique within its scope. Required.                                                                                       |
| **Description**           | Free text. Optional.                                                                                                                                     |
| **Scope**                 | **Personal** for a User environment, or **Shared with everyone** for a Global one. Only administrators see the second choice.                            |
| **Base image**            | The image the sandbox runs, for example `python:3.14`, `node:22` or `ubuntu:24.04`. Required.                                                            |
| **Environment variables** | Name and value pairs for the sandbox, each plain or secret. See [Environment variables](#environment-variables).                                         |
| **Repositories**          | The repositories the environment claims, as `owner/repo` or `group/subgroup/repo`. See [Repository bindings](#repository-bindings).                      |
| **Network**               | **Off** (the default) or **On**. **On** shows the **Network access** section. See [Network access and egress policy](#network-access-and-egress-policy). |
| **Resources**             | Expand it to set **Memory** and **CPUs**. Each is **Use default** or **Custom**.                                                                         |
| **Memory**                | A whole number of at least 1, with the unit **MiB** or **GiB**.                                                                                          |
| **CPUs**                  | A number of at least 0.25, in steps of 0.25.                                                                                                             |

**Use default** leaves **Memory** or **CPUs** unset, so the value comes from the global default environment. If that sets none either, DAIV asks for no limit. On the global default itself, the option reads **Unconstrained**. **Network** never comes from the global default: each environment sets its own.

## Change an environment

Changing an environment replaces the sandbox

A change to the base image, memory, CPUs, environment variables or egress policy replaces the sandbox of every existing session that uses the environment, on that session's next turn. The new sandbox starts from the repository, so anything installed in the old one, and anything a stopped turn left uncommitted, is lost.

To change an environment:

1. In **Sandbox environments**, select **Edit** next to the environment.
1. Change the fields, as in [Create an environment](#create-an-environment).
1. Select **Save**.

DAIV replaces a session's sandbox when the environment the turn resolves to differs from the one the sandbox started from. The comparison uses the environment merged over the global default, so switching the session to another environment, or changing the global default, replaces the sandbox too. DAIV updates a new git token on the running sandbox instead of replacing it.

## Delete an environment

Deleting cannot be undone

Deleting an environment destroys its stored environment variables and credentials. Sessions that recorded it fall back to the global default, which replaces their sandboxes on their next turn.

1. In **Sandbox environments**, select **Delete** next to the environment.
1. Select **Delete** to confirm `Delete environment "<name>"?`.

## Environment variables

Each variable has a name and a value. A name is a shell identifier: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit. An environment has at most 100 variables, and the encrypted values together may not exceed 32 KiB.

- Select **+ Add variable** to add a row, or **Paste .env** to import lines such as `KEY=value`. DAIV skips comments and blank lines, and you choose whether to merge (names that already exist are kept) or to replace all current variables.
- Set a row's toggle to **Secret** to hide its value. DAIV never shows a stored secret again: the dashboard shows the placeholder `🔒 keep existing`, and API and MCP responses show `******`. When you save, a secret keeps its stored value unless you type a new one.

DAIV encrypts the values with Fernet before it stores them and decrypts them when a run needs them, using `DAIV_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (see [Environment variables](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#external-url-and-encryption-key)). If the key changes and DAIV can no longer decrypt the stored values, the form refuses to save until you re-enter every secret value. Agent runs continue without the unreadable variables.

## Network access and egress policy

An environment with **Network** set to **Off** has no outbound network access. With **Network** set to **On**, the sandbox reaches only the hosts the **Network access** section allows, through the egress proxy of daiv-sandbox. The proxy can add a credential to a request, so a credential never enters the sandbox.

The egress proxy needs a CA certificate and key on the sandbox service (see [Deployment files](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/env-variables/#deployment-files)). Without them, a run that uses an environment with **Network** **On** stops instead of running with unrestricted network access.

DAIV runs git, including the push that publishes a run, from inside the sandbox. So DAIV always allows the run's git platform (GitLab or GitHub) and authenticates it with a short-lived token that the git platform mints at DAIV's request for the run, even when **Network** is **Off**. You never list it. Otherwise a **Network** **Off** environment stays isolated, and the git platform is opened only when the run holds a push token, so evaluation runs without one stay fully isolated.

### Allowed hosts

**Allowed hosts** lists one rule per host:

| Control                          | Meaning                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Host field                       | A host name or a glob such as `pypi.org` or `*.github.com`. Select **+ Add host** to add a rule.                   |
| **All methods** or **Read-only** | The HTTP methods the rule covers. **Read-only** covers `GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS`.                                |
| **+ credential**                 | An HTTP header name, such as `Authorization`, and a value. The proxy adds the header to every request to the host. |

**Unlisted hosts** sets what happens to a request that matches no rule:

- **Deny** blocks it.
- **Allow** lets it through.

With **Network** **On**, the policy must permit something. DAIV rejects a policy that has no allowed host and sets **Unlisted hosts** to **Deny**, with `Network is On but the egress policy permits nothing. Add at least one allowed host, set the default to allow, or switch Network to Off.` To block all general outbound traffic, set **Network** to **Off**. DAIV then stores no egress policy.

The proxy always inspects the TLS traffic of every reachable host, which is what lets it add credentials and enforce the method rules. You cannot turn that off.

DAIV encrypts credential values with Fernet before it stores them, and never sends them back to the browser or in an API or MCP response. A saved credential shows the placeholder `🔒 keep existing`, and saving keeps it unless you type a new value. An environment has at most 100 allowed-host rules and 100 credentials, and the encrypted credentials together may not exceed 32 KiB. A credential header name must be a valid HTTP header name, and its value cannot contain a line break.

If DAIV cannot decrypt an environment's egress credentials at run time, or its egress configuration is invalid, the run starts with no network access.

## Repository bindings

The **Repositories** field lists the repositories the environment claims. To add one, type `owner/repo` or `group/subgroup/repo` and select **+ Add**. When a run targets a claimed repository and no environment is selected, DAIV picks this one (see [How an environment is resolved](#how-an-environment-is-resolved)).

A repository can be claimed by one environment per scope. For User environments, that means one of your own. DAIV rejects a binding that overlaps another environment of the same scope and names that environment. The same repository can still appear in one User environment and one Global environment, and the User one wins.

## How an environment is resolved

When a run is requested, DAIV picks its environment for each repository in this order, records the choice on the run, and a session keeps the environment of its first run:

1. **Selected environment.** An environment chosen for the run overrides everything below. See [Choose an environment for a run](#choose-an-environment-for-a-run).
1. **User binding.** Your User environment that claims the repository.
1. **Global binding.** A Global environment that is not the default and that claims the repository.
1. **Global default.** The Global environment marked as default.
1. **None.** The run has no sandbox, and the agent gets no `bash` tool.

```
flowchart TD
    A[Run requested for a repo] --> B{Environment<br/>selected?}
    B -- Yes --> Z[Use it]
    B -- No --> C{User env binds<br/>this repo?}
    C -- Yes --> Z
    C -- No --> D{Global env binds<br/>this repo?}
    D -- Yes --> Z
    D -- No --> E{Global default<br/>exists?}
    E -- Yes --> Z
    E -- No --> F[No sandbox]
```

Runs that a webhook starts, such as [issue addressing](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/index.md), skip step 2: DAIV does not match User environments for them, even when the author has a DAIV account. They start at step 3.

DAIV then merges the chosen environment over the global default to get the effective runtime. The chosen environment wins for the base image, memory and CPUs when it sets a value, and the global default fills the rest. The environment variables of both are combined, and the chosen environment's variables replace same-named ones of the default. The egress policy is the exception: it comes from the chosen environment alone, so an environment with **Network** **Off** never inherits the default's policy.

The run starts from the recorded choice, so changing a binding afterwards moves no existing run. A run that a session's inbox starts, such as a [pipeline watch](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pipeline-watch/index.md) CI fix, uses the environment recorded on the session. For a run on behalf of someone else, such as a reply to another person's mention, DAIV never uses the session owner's User environment. It resolves one for that person instead: their own, a repository binding, or the global default. A session with no recorded environment, because its publishing run had none, it started before any environment existed, or its environment was deleted, runs on the global default.

## Choose an environment for a run

You do not have to bind an environment to a repository, because you can select one for a run. A selected environment always wins. Each surface has its own control, described on its page:

- The run composer and the chat workspace, in [Sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/index.md): the environment pill in the run composer, and the **Environment** field in the chat workspace. Both stay on **Auto** until you choose.
- A schedule, in [Scheduled jobs](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/scheduled-jobs/index.md): pin every run of the schedule to one environment.
- The `environment` field of `POST /api/jobs`, in the [Jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md).
- The `environment` argument of the `submit_job` tool, in the [MCP endpoint](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/mcp-endpoint/index.md), which also has the `list_environments` and `get_environment` tools to look environments up.

**Auto** means DAIV resolves the environment as above.

# Integrations

# Request Tracker triage

DAIV triages each new Request Tracker (RT) ticket as soon as it is created. The DAIV agent reads the ticket and classifies it as a bug, a configuration issue, a how-to question or unclear. When the ticket is code-related, the agent also runs a root-cause analysis against the queue's repository. DAIV posts the report on the ticket as an **internal comment**: staff-only, and not emailed to the requester.

The whole integration is a single RT scrip. It needs no bridge service, no webhook receiver and no polling.

## How it works

When a ticket is created, RT runs the scrip. The scrip looks up the queue's repository and submits a job to DAIV's jobs API. DAIV's agent then loads the ticket through the RT MCP server, triages it, and posts the report on the ticket through the same server.

```
RT ticket Create
      │
      ▼
RT scrip (Perl, "On Create", applies to allow-listed queues)
   1. Resolve queue → repo_id
   2. Build prompt (ticket id, url, queue, subject)
   3. POST $DAIV_URL/api/jobs
      │
      ▼
DAIV agent runs asynchronously
   - Reads the full ticket via its RT MCP tool
   - Does triage; if code-related, performs RCA against the repo
   - Posts the report as an internal comment on the ticket via RT MCP
```

The scrip is fire-and-forget. It submits the job with a 5-second socket timeout and a 10-second hard wall-clock ceiling (through `alarm`), and it traps any `die` from the HTTP client or the JSON parser in `eval`. A DAIV outage, including a DNS failure or a malformed response, never blocks or aborts the ticket-create transaction.

## Prerequisites

- A DAIV deployment that the RT host can reach, with the [jobs API](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/index.md).
- The RT MCP server added to DAIV as an MCP server (see [Add a server](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/mcp-tools/#add-a-server)). The RT MCP server must authenticate as an RT user with rights to **comment** on the target queues. A dedicated `daiv-bot` RT user keeps the comments clearly attributed.
- A system default model in DAIV, or an `agent_model` in the scrip's request. The scrip sends no `agent_model`, and DAIV refuses a job with `400` when no model is available (see [Error responses](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#error-responses)).
- A DAIV API key for a dedicated service user, with write access to every repository you map. See [Create an API key](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#create-an-api-key).

DAIV shows an API key once

The key has the form `prefix.secret`. Store it when you create it: you cannot retrieve it later.

To create the key from the command line for a service user named `rt-triage`:

```
docker compose exec app django-admin create_api_key rt-triage --name rt-scrip
```

## Configure RT

### Add the DAIV endpoint and key to `RT_SiteConfig.pm`

1. Open `RT_SiteConfig.pm` on the RT host.

1. Add these lines:

   ```
   Set($DAIV_URL,     'https://daiv.example.com');
   Set($DAIV_API_KEY, 'prefix.secret');
   ```

1. Reload RT, for example with `apache2ctl graceful`, or whichever reload command your RT host uses.

Replace `https://daiv.example.com` with your DAIV base URL and `prefix.secret` with the API key.

### Install the scrip

1. In the RT web UI, open **Admin** → **Scrips** → **Create**.

1. Enter these values:

   | Field       | Value                                                                                    |
   | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | Description | `DAIV triage on create`                                                                  |
   | Condition   | `On Create`                                                                              |
   | Action      | `User Defined`                                                                           |
   | Template    | `Blank`                                                                                  |
   | Stage       | `TransactionCreate`                                                                      |
   | Applies To  | *(leave empty; you set it in [Attach the scrip to queues](#attach-the-scrip-to-queues))* |

1. In **Custom action preparation code**, enter `return 1;`.

1. In **Custom action cleanup code**, paste the body of [`rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/integrations/rt/rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl). Cleanup runs after RT commits the ticket transaction, so the agent can load the new ticket through the RT MCP server.

1. In the pasted code, edit the `%QUEUE_REPO_MAP` hash at the top, so that each queue you want triaged maps to its DAIV `repo_id`, for example `group/project`.

1. Leave **Custom condition** empty.

1. Save the scrip.

A queue can map to several repositories. To have one agent session work across them, send them as one `repos` list with `"shared_session": true`. Without `shared_session`, each repository runs as a separate job. See [Multi-repository sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#multi-repository-sessions).

### Attach the scrip to queues

The **Applies To** list and the keys of `%QUEUE_REPO_MAP` must stay in lockstep. For a queue where the scrip runs but no repository is mapped, the scrip logs a warning and skips the ticket: it changes nothing and submits no job.

Start with a single pilot queue, and add more only after the pilot looks healthy.

1. In the RT admin UI, open the scrip's **Applies To** tab.
1. Select the pilot queue.
1. Save the change.

## Verify the pilot

1. File a test ticket in the pilot queue.

1. Follow the RT log, for example with `tail -f /var/log/request-tracker4/rt.log`, or your RT log path.

1. Look for this line:

   ```
   daiv-triage: submitted job <uuid> (batch <uuid>) for ticket <id> (queue=... repo=...)
   ```

1. In DAIV, open **Sessions** and confirm that a new `API Run` session exists for the target repository.

1. Wait a minute or two for an internal comment with the triage report to appear on the ticket.

If no comment appears, check the session's detail page: the agent may have failed mid-run, or failed to post through the RT MCP server.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                                        | Likely cause                                                                             | Fix                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| No log line at all after ticket create                         | The scrip is not attached to the queue, or its condition or stage is wrong               | Re-check the scrip's **Applies To** list, and confirm Condition=`On Create` and Stage=`TransactionCreate`                                                                                                                                                          |
| `DAIV_URL or DAIV_API_KEY not set` in `rt.log`                 | RT did not reload `RT_SiteConfig.pm`                                                     | Reload RT, for example with `apache2ctl graceful`                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `queue '<name>' in Applies-To but missing from QUEUE_REPO_MAP` | **Applies To** and the inline map drifted apart                                          | Add the queue to `%QUEUE_REPO_MAP` with its repository, or remove it from **Applies To**                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `failed to submit job … 401`                                   | Wrong or expired DAIV API key                                                            | Create a new key with [`create_api_key`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/management-commands/#create_api_key) and update `RT_SiteConfig.pm`                                                                                                               |
| `failed to submit job … 400`                                   | The request names no `agent_model`, and DAIV has no system default model                 | Set a system default model, or add `agent_model` to the scrip's request. A model set only in `.daiv.yml` does not count                                                                                                                                            |
| `rate-limited for ticket … 429` (warning)                      | The jobs API rate limit was exceeded                                                     | Raise the rate (see [Rate limiting](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#rate-limiting)), or give each queue its own API-key user (see [Cost considerations](#cost-considerations)). The scrip logs it at `warning`, so you can alert on `error` only |
| `failed to submit job … <other non-2xx>`                       | DAIV returned a 4xx or 5xx other than a rate limit                                       | Check the DAIV sessions list and access log. The log line holds the status line and body                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `exception in triage scrip: daiv-triage timeout`               | The 10-second hard ceiling tripped, usually on DNS resolution or a stalled TLS handshake | Check DNS and the network from the RT host to `$DAIV_URL`, and the certificate chain if you use HTTPS                                                                                                                                                              |
| `exception in triage scrip: <other>`                           | An unexpected `die` from LWP, the RT ticket object or elsewhere                          | Inspect `rt.log` around the timestamp: the captured `$@` points at the source                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| The job completes in DAIV but the ticket has no comment        | The RT MCP server's RT user lacks comment rights on the queue, or the MCP call failed    | Grant that user the `CommentOnTicket` right on the queue, and inspect the run's tool calls in the session detail                                                                                                                                                   |

## Cost considerations

The scrip sends `agent_thinking_level: high`, which asks for high reasoning effort. This gives better triage and costs more. The scrip sends no `agent_model`, so the run uses the model DAIV resolves for the repository (see [Model overrides](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/repository-config/#model-overrides)). To force the most capable model, also send an explicit `agent_model` in the scrip. See the [request fields](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#request-fields) of the jobs API.

For high-volume queues:

- Lower or omit `agent_thinking_level` in the scrip body for a cheaper first pass.
- Give each queue its own DAIV API-key user, so one busy queue cannot use up another's allowance. The jobs API applies one site-wide rate to each user separately, and you cannot set it lower for one user (see [Rate limiting](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/jobs-api/#rate-limiting)).

## Files

- [`rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl`](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/integrations/rt/rt-daiv-triage.scrip.pl): the scrip body to paste.
# Customization

# Repository configuration

A `.daiv.yml` file in the root of a repository's default branch changes how DAIV behaves in that repository: who can trigger it, which features run, and which models it uses. A repository without the file uses the defaults on this page and the site-wide settings.

## Full example

```
# Repository settings
default_branch: main
context_file_name: "AGENTS.md"
suggest_context_file: true
session_link: true

# Access control
allowed_usernames:
  - alice
  - bob

# Files whose diff content the commit and merge request writer does not see
omit_content_patterns:
  - "*.min.js"
  - "*.svg"
  - "*.lock"

# Feature toggles
issue_addressing:
  enabled: true

pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: true

slash_commands:
  enabled: true

pipeline_watch:
  enabled: true
  max_attempts: 3

orchestration:
  enabled: false

memory:
  enabled: true

# Model overrides
models:
  agent:
    model: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
    fallback_model: "openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol"
    thinking_level: "medium"
  diff_to_metadata:
    model: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
    fallback_model: "openrouter:openai/gpt-6.1-sol"
  skills:
    code-review: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
  subagents:
    cr-security: "openrouter:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5"
```

## How DAIV reads the file

DAIV always reads `.daiv.yml` from the platform's default branch, whatever the `default_branch` option says. It caches the file for 1 hour per repository, and a push to the default branch clears the cache, so a change you merge takes effect after that push. If the file is missing, DAIV uses the defaults. If DAIV cannot parse the file or one of its values, it logs an error and uses the defaults for the whole file. Model entries under `models.skills` and `models.subagents` are the exception: DAIV checks them when a run uses them, so a typo there never drops the rest of the file.

## Repository settings

| Option                 | Type          | Default            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------------- | ------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `default_branch`       | `str \| null` | Repository default | Base branch for merge requests.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `context_file_name`    | `str \| null` | `"AGENTS.md"`      | Name of the [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) guidance file. Set to `null` to disable.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `suggest_context_file` | `bool`        | `true`             | Suggest creating the context file when DAIV opens a merge request and the file is missing. See [AGENTS.md suggestion](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/#agentsmd-suggestion).                                                                      |
| `session_link`         | `bool`        | `true`             | Link back to the DAIV sessions that produced the changes, from the description of merge requests DAIV opens and from a `DAIV-Session` trailer on every commit. See [Linking back to sessions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/sessions/#linking-back-to-sessions). |

The context file tells DAIV about your repository's structure, conventions and constraints. Generate one with the `/init` skill; see [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/#init). For branch names and commit messages, see [Set branch and commit conventions](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/customization/agent-skills/#set-branch-and-commit-conventions).

`suggest_context_file` and `session_link` also have site-wide switches in [Site configuration](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/reference/site-configuration/index.md). DAIV applies them only when both the repository and the site allow them, so `true` here cannot turn on a feature the site turned off.

## Access control

Access control restricts which users can interact with DAIV on this repository. It matters most on public repositories, where you want to stop arbitrary users from triggering DAIV.

| Option              | Type        | Default | Description                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ----------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `allowed_usernames` | `list[str]` | `[]`    | Usernames allowed to interact with DAIV. When empty, all users are allowed. |

```
allowed_usernames:
  - alice
  - bob
  - charlie
```

When the list is empty or omitted, all users can interact with DAIV. When it lists users, only they can trigger DAIV through issues, comments and merge request reviews. Username matching is case-insensitive.

Warning

The allowlist decides who can **trigger** DAIV, not who it reads. On a merge request a DAIV session owns, a comment that doesn't mention DAIV is remembered from anyone and shown to that session's next run as context (see [Pull request assistant](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pull-request-assistant/#a-merge-request-daiv-published)). On a public repository, treat those comments as untrusted input.

## Omitted diff content

`omit_content_patterns` lists files whose changes stay in the diff, but whose content DAIV replaces with a placeholder before the diff reaches the model that writes commit messages and merge request descriptions. It keeps large generated files out of that model's input.

| Option                  | Type        | Default                                                        | Description                                                                                               |
| ----------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `omit_content_patterns` | `list[str]` | `["*package-lock.json", "*pnpm-lock.yaml", "*.lock", "*.svg"]` | Path patterns whose diff content is left out of generated commit messages and merge request descriptions. |

Patterns follow [fnmatch](https://docs.python.org/3/library/fnmatch.html) syntax and match against the file's path in the repository.

## Feature toggles

All features are on by default. To turn one off, set its `enabled` option to `false`:

```
issue_addressing:
  enabled: false

pull_request_assistant:
  enabled: false

slash_commands:
  enabled: false
```

| Section                  | Option         | Default   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------ | -------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `issue_addressing`       | `enabled`      | `true`    | [Issue addressing](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/issue-addressing/index.md)                                                                                                                |
| `pull_request_assistant` | `enabled`      | `true`    | [Pull request assistant](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pull-request-assistant/index.md)                                                                                                    |
| `slash_commands`         | `enabled`      | `true`    | [Slash commands and skills](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/slash-commands/index.md)                                                                                                         |
| `pipeline_watch`         | `enabled`      | `true`    | [Pipeline watch](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pipeline-watch/index.md): set it to `false` to stop DAIV watching CI on the merge requests it publishes.                                    |
| `pipeline_watch`         | `max_attempts` | site-wide | [Pipeline watch](https://docs.daivagent.com/dev/features/pipeline-watch/index.md): the maximum number of fix attempts before DAIV hands the merge request back. DAIV caps it at the site-wide limit. |
